newsitem.title: USA: Space station Mir has lifeboat ready.
newsitem.headline: Space station Mir has lifeboat ready.

text.p: The crew of the Russian Mir space station can evacuate their damaged orbital outpost at any time and a rescue by the U.S. space shuttle will not be needed, NASA officials said on Wednesday.
The station is equipped with a three-man Russian Soyuz spacecraft that could leave the station quickly and return to Earth within a day.
"There is no need for the shuttle, as the Soyuz can be used if necessary," NASA spokesman Joel Wells said.
NASA officials said an evacuation of the station was not planned.
In Russia, Mission Control Director Vladimir Lobachyov, speaking after liaising with the three-man Mir crew, told reporters that the collision was "the most serious accident in recent times."
The crew said they were facing power problems following the collision.
Shuttle Atlantis is not scheduled to visit Mir until September and the shuttle Columbia, which is being readied for launch on Tuesday, is not equipped for a Mir docking.
"Atlantis is the only shuttle configured for docking with Mir," said Wells, adding there were no plans to move up the launch date of Atlantis.
U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger and his Russian crewmates had to prepare to abandon ship twice during his four-month stay on Mir, which ended in May.
His crew first considered an evacuation during a serious fire in February and were again ready to leave when an off-course Progress craft was on a collision course with the station in March.

In an interview with Reuters this month, Linenger described his four-month stay on Mir as a fight for survival that left him frustrated because he was not always able to complete scientific experiments.
When a chemical oxygen generator burst into flame -- shooting sparks and molten metal across one of Mir's seven modules -- the sprawling station filled with thick, choking smoke, he said.

The blaze blocked the route to one of two Soyuz escape ships, which each seat three people. At the time there were six crew on board. One Soyuz was prepared for an emergency departure, but Linenger said there was never any thought of leaving half the crew behind.
Linenger also was aboard Mir when the crew lost control of the Progress cargo carrier in March, which he described as "a very tense moment."
"It looked like it was coming very fast and it looked like it was coming directly at us," he said. The craft veered off at the last moment.

NASA spokesman Ed Campion said Wednesday's collision with an unmanned cargo craft forced the crew to seal off the damaged module to stop a leakage of air pressure, but he said the current crew -- British-born NASA astronaut Michael Foale and Russian cosmonauts Vasily Tsibliev and Alexander Lazutkin -- were in no immediate danger.
